b: Developed through a joint initiative involving A-Insinöörit, Jatke, Metsä Wood, Saint-Gobain Finland and Würth, the system combines prefabricated wall and floor elements with thinner structural designs.
A new prefabricated system developed by five Finnish companies aims to improve the efficiency and cost competitiveness of wooden apartment construction

A new system developed in Finland could bring the construction of wooden apartment buildings closer to the efficiency of concrete ones, shortening construction time by up to 10% and reducing the thickness of structural elements. For a project with a one-year construction period, this could mean completion around five weeks earlier.

The system involves manufacturing apartment partition walls and intermediate floors as prefabricated elements in factories before delivering them to construction sites ready for installation. It also allows wall structures to be up to 30% thinner and intermediate floors 10–20% thinner than conventional wooden solutions.

The competitiveness of wooden apartment buildings has been constrained by factors including thicker structural elements and the amount of work required on site. To address these challenges, A-Insinöörit, Jatke, Metsä Wood, Saint-Gobain Finland and Würth collaborated to develop a prefabricated element system, which was presented for the first time at Puupäivät in Helsinki on 12 Nov 2026.

“The competitiveness of wooden construction cannot be solved with a single material or product. It is essential to examine the entire construction method. We have combined several Finnish product innovations into a functional structural system that brings wooden apartment building construction close to the efficiency of concrete construction in terms of both construction time and costs,” said Jesse Lietzén, regional director at A-Insinööriet, who led the product development project.
Apartment walls and floors installed in less than an hour
Partition walls and intermediate floors are manufactured in factory conditions and delivered to construction sites ready for installation

The solution has been piloted at a Jatke wooden apartment building project in Kirkkonummi, where the installation of partition wall and floor elements for one apartment was completed in less than an hour.

“Increasing industrial prefabrication is of great importance for both the speed and predictability of construction. With our prefabricated element solution, the number of work stages on the construction site is reduced, construction becomes more efficient and economics are improved. A wooden apartment building can be a truly competitive and attractive alternative to a concrete apartment building,” said Mika Airaksela, director at Jatke.

In conventional wooden apartment construction, load-bearing timber structures are installed first, followed by on-site work such as the cladding of walls and floors. Constructing sound-insulating suspended ceilings beneath intermediate floors is particularly labour-intensive.

The new system transfers much of this work to the factory. The load-bearing frames in the wall and floor structures use Metsä Wood’s veneered Kerto-Ripa wall and floor elements. The floor structures also incorporate the Kerto-Ripa Hybrid solution and Saint-Gobain’s Weber floor screed.

Another key component is a system based on Würth’s W-AKU partition wall bracket, which enables walls and partition walls to be manufactured as prefabricated elements. The system’s acoustic insulation, load-bearing capacity and fire safety have been verified in A-Insinöörit’s digital laboratory.
Thinner structures increase usable floor area
The system uses thinner veneered timber wall and floor elements, helping to increase usable floor area and reduce overall construction time

Through the use of thinner veneered timber partition walls and intermediate floors, structures built with the new system can be thinner than their concrete equivalents. Reducing structural thickness can also improve construction economics by increasing the net usable floor area and allowing for lower floor-to-floor heights.

“Our goal was not only to develop a slightly better wooden apartment building, but also to remove the practical obstacles that have so far weakened the competitiveness of wood in apartment building construction. When the construction method is standardised, completely new opportunities will open up for wood construction,” said Janne Heikkilä, director at Metsä Wood.
The system could create opportunities for Finland’s wood products industry, including the export of industrial timber construction solutions.
